\section{How Brokers Accumulate Informational and Structural Advantage: A Formal Illustration}

\subsection{Model and Methods}

I use an agent-based model (ABM) to formalize the theory. The model is an illustration, not a test of the theory; it serves as a bridge from theory to testable propositions. Complete pseudocode and specifications appear in Appendices A and B. The public git repository (\texttt{https://github.com/m-laprise/brokerage-abm}) contains the Julia code and scripts needed to reproduce the simulations, statistics, figures, and manuscript text.

The model isolates the informational consequences of outsourced relational work. Principals learn only from their own matches, whereas the broker pools information from matches it mediates across principals. Learning to evaluate general quality corresponds with attributional assessment, while learning to evaluate complementarity corresponds with relational assessment. The broker represents the information-aggregating function of corporate brokerage, not its internal organization, and the model does not simulate the later transition to resource capture or data enclosure.

\emph{Market and match output}. Principals are the market participants seeking partners. Many principals and one broker occupy an undirected network. Each principal has a fixed vector of observable characteristics, which defines its type. At baseline, types are drawn around a smooth curve in an eight-dimensional space of observable characteristics (Supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:supp-type-geometry}). For any potential pair, expected match output is determined by the two principals' types and by fixed features of the matching environment drawn at the start of each simulation run. A match's output combines two components: general quality, which depends on each principal separately, and complementarity, which depends on how their types interact (Appendix B \S2). Under pure general quality, a higher-quality counterparty raises expected output for every principal. With complementarity, expected output also depends on which two principals are paired (Supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:supp-dgp-structure}).

Before they are combined, the components are centered and scaled to have the same variance. The parameter $\rho$ sets their relative contributions to variation in expected match output: general quality contributes a fraction $\rho$, and complementarity contributes $1-\rho$. Thus, $\rho=0$ represents pure complementarity and $\rho=1$ represents pure general quality. The parameter $\delta$ controls the difficulty of learning complementarity by varying how sharply complementarity changes across an arbitrary boundary in type-pair space: it multiplies complementarity by $1+\delta$ on one side and $1-\delta$ on the other. Larger values make otherwise similar pairs on opposite sides of the boundary differ more in expected output. A common normalization holds the average within-market variance of expected match output constant as $\rho$ and $\delta$ vary. Because $\delta$ affects only complementarity, it has no effect when $\rho=1$. Describing variation in expected output across pairs requires more dimensions under complementarity than under pure general quality, particularly when difficulty is high (Supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:supp-dgp-dimension}).

When a pair matches, its realized output equals its expected output plus an independent, mean-zero random shock. This shock represents match-specific variation that neither the principals nor the broker can anticipate.

\emph{Search, matching, and learning}. Each period, principals seek pairwise matches either through self-search or through the broker (Appendix A \S\S5--7; Appendix B \S\S6--7). They choose one channel using satisfaction with past realized output net of search costs or broker fees. Self-search considers existing neighbors and a small random sample of other principals. The broker considers principals in its standing roster (a persistent list of contacts), and those currently using its services.

Principals and the broker accumulate observations and learn in parallel. After every completed match, each principal records its partner's characteristics and the realized output, whether the match was arranged through self-search or through the broker. The broker also records both parties' characteristics and realized output from every match it mediates, pooling observations across clients. It does not observe matches arranged entirely through self-search.

Each principal uses its own observations to predict the output of matching with a candidate, using that candidate's characteristics. The broker uses its pooled observations to predict output from both parties' characteristics. In the main variant, each principal has its own neural network, and the broker has a separate neural network. In another variant, these predictions use Ridge regression.

Estimated output determines how candidates are ranked. For previously matched neighbors, self-search instead uses the pair's average past realized output. Tied estimates are ordered uniformly at random. Principals make offers to the highest-ranked candidates whose estimated output exceeds the reservation threshold, the minimum required for an offer. All offers enter a common market. A completed match creates a direct tie that persists until either principal exits. At the end of each period, every principal exits independently with probability $\eta$ and is replaced by a new entrant.

\emph{Measurement}. The outsourcing rate is the share of requested match positions routed through the broker. A brokered placement is classified as access when it creates a direct tie between previously unconnected principals and as assessment when it reuses an existing tie. The access fraction is the share of brokered placements classified as access. The output gap is the difference in mean realized output between brokered matches and self-search matches. Net output to principals is realized output net of search costs and broker fees, averaged over all requested match positions, including those that remain unfilled. Broker betweenness centrality measures the share of shortest paths between principals that pass through the broker (Brandes 2001; Freeman 1977). Supplementary Figures~\ref{fig:supp-grid}--\ref{fig:supp-advantage} reproduce the structural analyses using Burt's constraint and effective size instead of betweenness centrality.

Prediction quality is evaluated each period using randomly sampled potential partners. These evaluations do not update either model. Predictions are compared with the expected output, without random shock. Rank correlation is Spearman's correlation between the candidate ordering produced by the predicted output and the ordering produced by the expected output. The ranking advantage is the broker's rank correlation minus the principals' rank correlation (Appendix B \S8).

\emph{Simulation design and analysis}. At the baseline, $N=1{,}000$ principals interact for $T=500$ periods with $\rho=0.5$, $\delta=0.5$, and $\eta=0.02$. One-at-a-time (OAT) sweeps vary the matching problem, turnover, market size, reservation threshold, initial network, broker roster, and self-search pool. Four two-parameter grids cross $\rho$ with $\eta$, $\rho$ with the reservation threshold, $\eta$ with the reservation threshold, and $\rho$ with $\delta$ (Appendix B \S9). I refer to each unique model configuration as a regime. Together, the sweeps and grids contain \pv{nRegimes} regimes. There are \pv{nGeneralSeeds} random seeds per regime and \pv{nBaselineSeeds} at the baseline (\pv{nRuns} runs total).

Neural-network performance depends on the learning rate and the number of training updates, which were calibrated before running the main simulations. I compared candidate settings for principals and the broker separately, considering ranking performance on randomly sampled candidates, stability over time and across random seeds, and computational time.

To show that the findings do not depend on neural-network learning, I repeat the complete design with Ridge regression. In the unrestricted Ridge specification, principals use candidate characteristics, while the broker uses both parties' characteristics and interactions between them. Ridge penalties were calibrated at the baseline using ranking performance on randomly sampled candidates. Three additional Ridge experiments, conducted at the baseline and across the $\rho\times\delta$ grid, restrict the broker by giving it the same number of observations as a typical principal, retaining only one party's characteristics from each match, or omitting interactions between the two parties' characteristics.

Ensemble means are averages across random seeds. Window means are taken by first averaging over periods within seeds, and then averaging over seeds. Late-window is $t\in[481,500]$; early-window is $t\in[51,70]$. Cross-regime summaries give each regime equal weight. Intervals for differences are calculated within each random seed before being combined across seeds. Unless otherwise noted in a figure caption, time-series figures begin at $t=\pv{axisStart}$ to omit the initialization transient. Monte Carlo convergence was assessed in two ways. For each regime and reported outcome, I calculated a two-sided 95\% confidence interval for the mean across independent random seeds using the $t$ distribution. I also compared nested estimates based on the first 10 versus all 20 seeds outside the baseline and the first 20 versus all 50 seeds at the baseline. Across the \pv{mcOutcomeCount} outcomes included in the convergence summary, the median across regimes of the confidence-interval half-width divided by the absolute estimate based on all available seeds ranged from \pv{mcCiMedianMinPercent}\% to \pv{mcCiMedianMaxPercent}\%. The median across regimes of the absolute difference between the nested estimates, divided by the same full estimate, ranged from \pv{mcNestedMedianMinPercent}\% to \pv{mcNestedMedianMaxPercent}\%. These relative quantities are not reported when the full-sample interval includes zero to avoid division by near zero; those cases are assessed in the outcome's original units.

\emph{Assessment and access experiment}. To examine the value and structural consequences of assessment and access, I conduct an experiment comparing three versions of the single-broker model. Full service combines the broker's assessments with access to its contacts and current clients. Assessment-only uses the broker's assessments to rank candidates available through ordinary self-search. Access-only ranks the broker's broader candidate set using principals' own assessments. In each version, the broker still organizes matches, charges the same fee, and observes and learns from the matches it arranges.

Each simulation uses one broker model throughout. Changing the service changes matches, outsourcing, network formation, and subsequent learning. The comparisons therefore capture these combined effects.

\subsection{The Broker Primarily Provides Assessment, Not Access}

Across the tested regimes, the broker is usually the dominant channel in the market. The outsourcing rate as a share of demand is \pv{outBaselineLate} at the baseline (late mean, up from an early mean of \pv{outBaselineEarly}) and has a median of \pv{outBaseMed} across regimes. It exceeds one-half in \pv{outBaseDominantN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes; the remaining regimes all have no turnover. Yet the broker primarily assesses options within the existing network rather than providing access beyond it. The access fraction (the share of brokered placements between principals with no pre-existing tie) has a late mean of \pv{accessAcrossBaseLate} across regimes, down from \pv{accessAcrossBaseEarly} early, and never exceeds \pv{accessBaseMax}. \ifnum\pv{accessDeclineCIN}=\pv{nRegimes}\relax It declines over time in all regimes, and its paired 95\% interval is below zero in every regime.\else It declines significantly in \pv{accessDeclineCIN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes.\fi\ Most brokered matches therefore connect principals already tied to each other. Figure~\ref{fig:dynamics} and Table~\ref{tab:baseline-measures} summarize these baseline dynamics and the main measures.

At the baseline, the broker's realized-output advantage develops as the market evolves: the output gap (broker minus self-search) changes from $\pv{ogapBaselineEarly}$ early to $\pv{ogapBaselineLate}$ late. Across regimes, mean realized output is higher through the broker channel in \pv{ogapBasePosN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes, and the late output gap averages $\pv{ogapBaseMean}$. Paired 95\% Monte Carlo intervals are above zero in \pv{ogapBaseCIPosN} regimes and below zero in \pv{ogapBaseCINegN}. The negative gaps occur in \pv{ogapBaseNegN} regimes, all with no or nearly no turnover ($\eta\in\{0,0.001\}$). Principals choose a channel using satisfaction scores that include unfilled requests, fees, and search costs, whereas the output gap compares realized output among completed matches. Outsourcing is therefore not itself evidence that the broker always produces better matches.

The broker's assessment advantage appears more consistently in ranking candidates than in predicting expected output levels. Among randomly sampled potential partners (Appendix~A~\S8), its rank correlation is \pv{brokerRankBaseline} at the baseline and has a median of \pv{brokerRankBaseMed} across regimes, compared with \pv{agentRankBaseline} and \pv{agentRankBaseMed} for principals. The broker-minus-principal difference in rank correlation is positive in \pv{rankGapNNPosN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes, with paired 95\% intervals above zero in \pv{rankGapNNCiPosN} regimes. Ranking determines which candidates are considered first, while predicted levels also determine whether offers clear the reservation threshold. Accurate ranking is therefore more important than accurate prediction of expected output levels, although both can affect matching.

Most brokered placements therefore reuse ties that principals could search directly; relatively few expand the principal network. The broker's ranking advantage appears under pure general quality as well as complementarity: at $\rho=1$, the broker-minus-principal difference in rank correlation averages \pv{rhoOneRankGapMean} and is positive in all \pv{rhoOneRankGapPosN} pure-quality regimes. The OAT checks also show that initial network degree ($k_G$), broker roster fraction, and the number of strangers available in self-search have comparatively small effects on the main economic outcomes.

\subsection{The Value and Structural Consequences of Access and Assessment}
\label{sec:assessment-access}

The access fraction records how often brokered placements create new ties, but does not establish what makes brokerage valuable to principals. The assessment and access experiment examines these contributions by comparing full service with assessment-only and access-only service.

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/assessment_access_2.png}
\caption{\textbf{\pvtitle{assessment_access}.} \pvcaption{assessment_access}}
\label{fig:assessment-access}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Access Can Raise Output While Eroding Structural Advantage}

Access can add value even when most brokered placements reuse existing ties. At baseline turnover, net output is \pv{aaAccessOutputLoss} lower per requested position under assessment-only than under full service (Figure~\ref{fig:assessment-access}, Panel A). This advantage of full service depends on turnover. Without turnover, assessment-only produces more output than full service; at the tested rates of $\eta\in\{\pv{aaAccessLossEtas}\}$, it produces less. At $\eta=\pv{aaEtaSmall}$, the smallest positive rate tested, the difference is uncertain. The zero-turnover advantage of assessment-only and its losses at $\eta=\pv{aaEtaLower}$ and $\eta=\pv{aaEtaUpper}$ hold across all tested matching compositions (Supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:supp-assessment-access}, Panel B).

Turnover continually removes principals and relationships, making access to new counterparties useful. Without turnover, relationships accumulate, and candidates reachable through ordinary self-search can support valuable brokerage based on assessment alone. Broader access then provides no net-output advantage. The frequency of introductions alone therefore does not establish the value of access.

Access can also weaken the broker's structural position. Each successful introduction creates a direct tie that principals can use in later self-search. Providing that connection can therefore reduce the need to buy it again. The comparison with assessment-only supports this self-liquidating mechanism: full service produces higher mean principal degree and lower broker centrality in every tested condition. Principal degree counts each principal's ties, including its link to the broker when present.

At baseline turnover, mean principal degree initially rises and then declines under full service, whereas it continues to rise under access-only (Figure~\ref{fig:assessment-access}, Panel B). The access-only broker falls further behind full service in centrality over time (Panel D). Its mean centrality difference over the final \pv{aaLateWidth} periods is $\pv{aaAccessCentralityDifference}$ [$\pv{aaAccessCentralityLower}$, $\pv{aaAccessCentralityUpper}$] (Panel C). Over the same late period, mean principal degree is higher under access-only (\pv{aaAccessDegree} versus \pv{aaFullDegree}).

At baseline turnover, broker betweenness rises even under access-only service, as continued outsourcing connects principals to the broker. But it remains much lower than under assessment-only service (Panel D). Access therefore exerts a self-liquidating force without producing an absolute decline: introductions create direct ties among principals and erode the centrality the broker would otherwise accumulate. Turnover also removes ties and renews opportunities for brokerage. Because learning and outsourcing change with the service provided, these comparisons do not isolate the effect of new direct ties alone.

\subsubsection{Assessment Can Sustain Brokerage Without Additional Access}

Principals continue paying for brokerage even when it provides no additional access. At baseline turnover, they outsource \pv{aaAssessmentOutPercent}\% of requested positions to the assessment-only broker, compared with \pv{aaFullOutPercent}\% for full service and \pv{aaAccessOutPercent}\% for access-only. The assessment-only and full-service outsourcing rates remain close across the tested turnover conditions, though both fall to about half without turnover.

Adding assessment to access-only service raises outsourcing in every tested condition. Adding access to assessment-only service has smaller effects, sometimes positive and sometimes negative. Assessment is therefore more important than additional access for sustaining brokerage use in this experiment.

Continued outsourcing, however, reflects how brokerage compares with self-search. Principals may keep using the broker because its assessments improve matching, because their independent alternatives are less productive, or both.

The assessment-only broker is already more central than full service at the first measurement. Full service partly catches up over time (Panel D), but the assessment-only broker retains a late-mean centrality advantage of $\pv{aaAssessmentCentralityDifference}$ [$\pv{aaAssessmentCentralityLower}$, $\pv{aaAssessmentCentralityUpper}$] (Panel C). Mean principal degree remains lower than under either other broker model (Panel B), with a late mean of \pv{aaAssessmentDegree}.

Assessment contributes more to net output for principals than additional access in these comparisons. At baseline, adding assessment to access-only service raises net output per requested position by \pv{aaAssessmentOutputLoss}, compared with \pv{aaAccessOutputLoss} from adding access to assessment-only service (Panel A). Assessment-only therefore exceeds access-only by \pv{aaAssessmentAccessOutputDifference}, with a paired \pv{aaIntervalPercent}\% interval of [\pv{aaAssessmentAccessOutputLower}, \pv{aaAssessmentAccessOutputUpper}]. This advantage holds in every tested condition, with all paired intervals above zero.

Without the broker's assessments, access-only produces less net output than full service at every tested turnover rate, including zero. Both assessment and access become more valuable to principals as turnover rises. Between turnover rates of $\pv{aaEtaLower}$ and $\pv{aaEtaUpper}$, output changes little under full service but falls under both assessment-only and access-only.

At baseline, assessment-only has nearly the same outsourcing rate as full service and higher centrality, yet delivers less net output to principals. High centrality need not mean greater use, and neither alone establishes greater value for principals.

The assessment-only result also connects the formal illustration to data enclosure. The broker continues to create value when it assesses only candidates that principals could reach through ordinary self-search. Its information is therefore valuable independently of privileged access. The experiment does not model data enclosure itself, because the broker still mediates matches and learns from them. It nevertheless establishes its prerequisite: assessment can become a distinct service that could be unbundled from intermediation and sold as predictions or analytics.

\subsection{The Broker's Information Advantage Comes from Data Volume and Relational Information}

The theory identifies two sources of the broker's information advantage: the greater volume of observations generated by working across principals and relational information about both parties to each match. The Ridge experiments separate these sources from the flexibility of the neural network. When Ridge regression replaces both neural networks, the broker-minus-principal difference in rank correlation is \pv{ridgeBaselineGap} at the baseline, has a median of \pv{ridgeMedianGap} across the \pv{ridgeNConditions} regimes, and is positive in all \pv{ridgePositiveN}. The full Ridge model still gives the broker more observations and more information about each pair than a principal. Because each restriction changes later matching and learning, their effects need not be additive.

Data volume accounts for much of the advantage (Fig.~\ref{fig:information-sources}). Across the \pv{ablationConditionN} regimes in the baseline and $\rho\times\delta$ design, the median broker-minus-principal difference in rank correlation is \pv{ablationPairMedianGap} in the full Ridge model but only \pv{ablationSizeMedianGap} when the broker trains on the same number of observations as a typical principal. The difference remains positive in \pv{ablationSizePositiveN} of \pv{ablationConditionN} regimes under this restriction, so data volume is important without being the broker's only advantage.

The content of the broker's data also matters. When each observation retains the characteristics of only one party to a match, the broker's median advantage over principals in ranking new candidates is \pv{ablationSingleMedianGap} and remains positive in only \pv{ablationSinglePositiveN} of the \pv{ablationConditionN} tested regimes. Retaining both parties' characteristics improves on this one-party version in \pv{ablationAdditiveBeatsSingleN} of \pv{ablationConditionN} regimes, and retaining how those characteristics interact improves it further in \pv{ablationPairBeatsAdditiveN} of \pv{ablationConditionN} regimes. Interaction information matters most when complementarity contributes strongly to expected match output and not at all under pure general quality. The broker's advantage therefore comes from both the volume of observations generated through repeated vicarious relational work and information about how the characteristics of two parties combine.

In the assessment and access experiment, the access-only broker also develops an informational advantage. Although it uses principals' assessments to choose matches, it continues to record and learn from their outcomes. When tested on randomly sampled potential partners, its own predictions rank match quality more accurately than principals' predictions (baseline rank correlations of \pv{aaAccessBrokerRank} and \pv{aaAccessPrincipalRank}, respectively). Under the model's observation and learning rules, the broker thus gains an informational advantage even though it does not use its own assessments in matching. The assessment-only result shows that this capability can sustain a paid service without additional access.

\end{figure}

\subsection{The Nature of the Matching Problem Shapes the Broker's Advantage}
\label{sec:matching-shapes}

The full-service comparisons vary two features of the matching problem: whether expected match output depends on general quality or pair-specific complementarity, and how difficult complementarity is to learn. The parameter $\rho$ moves expected match output from pure complementarity at $\rho=0$ toward pure general quality at $\rho=1$. The parameter $\delta$ increases difficulty by making expected output change more sharply across a boundary in type-pair space. Because complementarity disappears at $\rho=1$, $\delta$ has no effect there. The pure-quality case is therefore a separate boundary condition, not a smooth continuation of the interior $\rho$ values.

Broker centrality is governed primarily by the composition of expected match output. In the one-at-a-time sweep from $\rho=0$ to $\rho=0.85$, the access fraction rises from \pv{accessRho0} to \pv{accessRho085} and broker betweenness centrality falls from \pv{betwRho0} to \pv{betwRho085}. The $\rho\times\eta$ grid shows the same directions at every turnover rate. At the pure-quality boundary, centrality falls further to \pv{betwRho1}, while access returns to \pv{accessRho1}. The boundary therefore extends the decline in centrality but not the increase in access below $\rho=1$.

Under pure complementarity, greater difficulty lowers the ranking accuracy of both the broker and principals, but it does not eliminate the broker's advantage. Increasing $\delta$ from 0 to 1 lowers the broker's rank correlation from \pv{brokerRankRho0D0} to \pv{brokerRankRho0D1} and the principal correlation from \pv{agentRankRho0D0} to \pv{agentRankRho0D1} (Fig.~\ref{fig:grid}). The corresponding broker-minus-principal differences are \pv{rankGapRho0D0} and \pv{rankGapRho0D1}. The size of this difference is not monotonic in difficulty, but its paired 95\% interval is above zero in \pv{gridRankGapCIPosN} of the \pv{rhoDeltaEffectiveN} regimes. Because $\delta$ changes only complementarity, it is inactive at the pure-quality boundary.

The broker's realized-output advantage is greatest when expected match output depends more heavily on complementarity. Paired 95\% intervals for the broker-minus-self-search output gap are above zero in \pv{gridOutputGapCIPosN} of the \pv{rhoDeltaEffectiveN} regimes. Composition and difficulty therefore shape different outcomes. Greater difficulty makes candidates harder for both sides to rank but does not produce a monotonic change in the broker's relative ranking advantage. Greater reliance on complementarity increases the mean realized output produced through brokered matches. The broker retains both a ranking advantage and an output advantage throughout the grid.

The assessment and access experiment provides direct evidence for this role of complementarity. At each turnover rate compared across matching compositions, adding the broker's assessments to access-only service produces a larger gain in net output under pure complementarity than under pure general quality (Supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:supp-assessment-access}). Complementarity therefore increases the value to principals of using the broker's assessments, beyond the access that the broker already provides.

\subsection{A Broker Can Be Highly Central While Doing Little Bridging}

In most full-service regimes, the broker's structural position strengthens over time while principals have fewer direct ties on average. At the baseline, mean principal degree falls from \pv{degBaselineEarly} to \pv{degBaselineLate}, while broker betweenness centrality rises from \pv{betwBaselineEarly} to \pv{betwBaselineLate} (early to late means; Fig.~\ref{fig:dynamics}). This combination occurs in \pv{comoveN} of \pv{nRegimes} regimes, and principal degree falls in \pv{degFallsN} of them. In most regimes, direct ties do not accumulate fast enough to offset turnover. The broker's structural advantage therefore does not disappear as brokered matches create direct ties. Because outsourcing connects current clients to the broker, sustained use converts the value of assessment into structural centrality.

The distinction between assessment and access helps explain this relationship. An access match creates a direct tie between previously unconnected principals and can remove the broker from their shortest path. An assessment match reuses an existing tie, so the broker can serve the market without directly adding ties to the principal network.

The assessment and access experiment provides direct evidence of these structural consequences. At baseline turnover, full service produces higher mean principal degree and lower broker centrality than assessment-only (Figure~\ref{fig:assessment-access}, Panels B--D). Providing access alongside assessment therefore strengthens principals' connectivity while weakening the broker's structural position.

This helps explain why the full-service broker usually gains centrality in the main simulations. As its work becomes increasingly assessment-based, relatively few brokered matches create new ties among principals. Valuable assessments sustain outsourcing, which connects principals to the broker, while turnover removes ties and renews opportunities for brokerage. The broker's structural position strengthens despite the self-liquidating force of its introductions.

Figure~\ref{fig:position} compares broker centrality with principal degree (Panel A) and access fraction (Panel B) across matching compositions and turnover rates. Holding turnover fixed, moving from pure complementarity toward $\rho=0.85$ raises access and lowers centrality. Holding $\rho$ fixed, increasing turnover raises both access and centrality at every tested $\rho$. Turnover creates network gaps, while matching composition determines how often brokerage closes them with direct ties.

The turnover effect is substantial but nonlinear (Panel A). Holding other parameters at baseline, increasing $\eta$ from 0 to 0.03 lowers late mean principal degree from \pv{degEta0Late} to \pv{degEta003Late} and raises broker centrality from \pv{betwEta0Late} to \pv{betwEta003Late}, with most of the change occurring between $\eta=0.001$ and $0.01$. Turnover also changes the broker's realized-output advantage. In the $\rho\times\eta$ grid, the 95\% interval for the broker-minus-self-search output gap is below zero in \pv{qgapEta0CINegN} of \pv{rhoEtaRhoN} $\rho$ conditions at $\eta=0$, but above zero in \pv{qgapEta01CIPosN} of \pv{rhoEtaRhoN} by $\eta=0.01$. In the model, turnover removes principals and ties, creating network gaps and the conditions under which brokered matches outperform self-search.

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/centrality_and_access.png}
\caption{\textbf{\pvtitle{position}.} \pvcaption{position}}
\label{fig:position}
\end{figure}

The pure-quality boundary confirms that low access alone is not sufficient for high centrality. Although higher turnover raises centrality there, centrality remains below pure complementarity at the same turnover rate. In the tested regimes, high centrality occurs when turnover renews network gaps and brokerage mainly assesses existing relationships.

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/structural_advantage.png}
\caption{\textbf{\pvtitle{advantage}.} \pvcaption{advantage}}
\label{fig:advantage}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:advantage} shows that structural position relates differently to relative ranking and realized match output. Holding all other parameters fixed, moving from pure complementarity to pure general quality reduces the output gap from \pv{ogapRho0Group} to \pv{ogapRho1Group}, while increasing the broker-minus-principal difference in rank correlation from \pv{rankGapRho0Group} to \pv{rankGapRho1Group}. The broker is therefore most central and produces its largest realized-output advantage where its advantage over principals in ranking candidates is smaller.

Repeated relational work generates information that can sustain the broker's assessment advantage. When those assessments remain valuable relative to self-search, principals continue outsourcing even when they can reach counterparties themselves. Sustained use converts the value of assessment into structural centrality. High centrality can therefore be a product of the broker's relational work rather than evidence of frequent bridging.

\subsection{Propositions}

The simulation results motivate the following falsifiable propositions for future empirical research:

\noindent\textbf{P1.} \textbf{\textit{Assessment is the primary source of brokerage value}}. In matching markets, brokers add value primarily by assessing counterparties rather than by bridging disconnected parties. The value of this assessment role increases as complementarity contributes more to match output.

\noindent\textbf{P2.} \textbf{\textit{Relationship disruption increases the value of access brokerage}}. Clients gain more from brokers' ability to find new counterparties when market participants frequently leave and are replaced than when they can rely on stable relationships.

\noindent\textbf{P3.} \textbf{\textit{When the broker records and accumulates data about his matching work, brokerage widens informational asymmetry}}. Repeated brokerage increases the broker's assessment advantage over his clients, even though those clients also learn from the matches he arranges.

\noindent\textbf{P4.} \textbf{\textit{Assessment brokerage produces high broker centrality with little bridging behavior}}. Sustained outsourcing converts the value of assessment into a greater structural centrality for the broker. Brokers whose assessments remain valuable relative to clients' independent alternatives become highly central even when most of their matches involve counterparties already connected to one another.

\noindent\textbf{P5.} \textbf{\textit{Assessment enables the broker to become a principal}}. Corporate brokers whose assessments create value independently of privileged access are more likely to use that capability on their own behalf, either to acquire and sell resources they previously intermediated (resource capture) or to sell predictions or analytics directly (data enclosure).
